Handstaves
HAND-stavz
n. pl. (hand-weapons; staves or javelins carried in the hand)
From hand and staves, the plural of staff — weapons held in the hand rather than thrown from an engine. The Authorized Version uses the word once, in Ezekiel's account of the burning of the weapons of Gog.

Biblical Definition

After the overthrow of Gog, they that dwell in the cities of Israel go forth and burn the weapons: the shields and the bucklers, the bows and the arrows, and the handstaves, and the spears, and they burn them with fire seven years. The inventory is deliberate. Ezekiel does not summarise; he lists the gear piece by piece as a quartermaster would, and the effect of the list is finality. Every category of weapon the invader brought is named and every one goes into the fire. The next verse presses the point into economics: they shall take no wood out of the field, neither cut down any out of the forests, for they shall burn the weapons with fire. The instruments of a great invasion become seven years of firewood, and the nation that was to be spoiled spoils those that spoiled them. Scripture's hope for the end of war is never disarmament by treaty. It is the LORD breaking the bow and cutting the spear in sunder and burning the chariot in the fire, and the beating of swords into plowshares happens when he shall judge among the nations, not before. Handstaves is a small word for that great settlement.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a staff borne in the hand, particularly as a weapon; in Scripture, among the arms of Gog burned by Israel for seven years.

expand to see more

HANDSTAFF, n. A javelin, or staff borne in the hand.

STAFF, n. A stick carried in the hand for support or defence; a weapon.

BUCKLER, n. A kind of shield, or piece of defensive armour, worn on the left arm.

SPEAR, n. A long pointed weapon, used in war and hunting, by thrusting or throwing.

SPOIL, v.t. To plunder; to strip by violence; to take by force from an enemy.

Key Scripture

Eze 39:9 — "And they that dwell in the cities of Israel shall go forth, and shall set on fire and burn the weapons, both the shields and the bucklers, the bows and the arrows, and the handstaves, and the spears, and they shall burn them with fire seven years:"

Eze 39:10 — "So that they shall take no wood out of the field, neither cut down any out of the forests; for they shall burn the weapons with fire: and they shall spoil those that spoiled them, and rob those that robbed them, saith the Lord GOD."

Isa 2:4 — "And he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more."

Psa 46:9 — "He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire."

Modern Corruption

Isaiah's swords into plowshares is quoted as a programme for human peacemaking with the judging Messiah cut out of the verse; in the text the disarmament follows the judgment and is its fruit.

expand to see more

Isaiah 2:4 is probably the most misquoted verse in the political vocabulary, engraved on walls with its first clause removed. The verse opens with a judge: and he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people. Only then do they beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruninghooks, and only then do they learn war no more. The peace is real and it is coming, and it arrives by the rebuke of Christ and not by the goodwill of the parties. Psalm 46 says the same in the same order: he maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow. The bow does not lay itself down.

Ezekiel 39 fills in what that looks like on the ground, and it is neither sentimental nor abstract. Somebody has to gather the handstaves and burn them, and it takes seven years, and there is a further seven months of burying the dead in the valley. Scripture is sober about the cost of the settlement it promises. The dictionary declines both the utopianism that expects the plowshares without the Judge and the fatalism that expects the wars without the end of them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew maqqel yad (H4731, H3027), a rod of the hand; neshek (H5402), weapons or armour; chaniyth (H2595), a spear.

expand to see more

Hebrew maqqel (H4731) — a rod, a staff, a stick; with yad, the handstaves of Ezekiel 39:9.

Hebrew yad (H3027) — a hand; the staff borne in it rather than cast from an engine.

Hebrew neshek (H5402) — military equipment, armour, weapons; what Israel burned.

Hebrew chaniyth (H2595) — a spear or lance; last in Ezekiel's inventory.

Hebrew shalal (H7997) — to plunder, to spoil; they shall spoil those that spoiled them.

Usage

"“the handstaves, and the spears” — the single occurrence, in the inventory of Gog's weapons."

"“they shall burn them with fire seven years” — an invasion reduced to firewood."

"“he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder” — who ends the wars."
